Backscatter mode¶

Summary¶

In backscatter mode the signal comes almost straight back toward where it came from. The transmitter, the surface point, and the receiver sit nearly on one straight line, so the wave is sent back along its own path (a retroreflection). This is the geometry of ordinary radar: a ship is a hard, strong scatterer that stands out against the weak return of the open sea.

Both analysis modes can use this geometry. Moving-target detection compares the modelled return from the ship against the modelled return from the sea around it, giving a deterministic ship-versus-sea ratio. Area coverage counts, per grid cell, the contiguous passes of the near-backscatter swath – all cells whose bistatic angle to some (Tx, Rx) pair stays below [COVERAGE].max_bistatic_bksc_angle_deg (see Coverage).

The geometry¶

The surface point is the Backscatter Reflection Point (BRP): the point where the straight line through the transmitter and the receiver meets the Earth on the receiver’s side. Writing that line through the transmitter \(T\) and receiver \(R\),

(5)¶\[\mathbf{P}(t) = T + t\,\hat{u}, \qquad \hat{u} = \frac{R - T}{\lVert R - T\rVert},\]

the BRP is the first place this line crosses the surface beyond the receiver. Putting \(\mathbf{P}(t)\) into the selected sphere or WGS-84 ellipsoid equation gives a quadratic in \(t\); the accepted root must satisfy \(t>\lVert R-T\rVert\). The full solve, the incidence angle, and the geometry gates are in Backscatter point / BRP.

The sea return¶

Looking straight back at the sea at oblique incidence, the bright quasi-specular scatter is gone – almost no facet is tilted steeply enough to bounce the signal straight back. What is left is Bragg scatter: a weak, resonant return from small wind-driven ripples whose wavelength matches the radar. The simulator carries both mechanisms: the quasi-specular geometric-optics term, which owns the steep (near-nadir) geometry, and the two-scale Bragg term of Ocean physics, gated on at incidence >= 20 deg where it dominates. The resulting cross-section per unit area (the NRCS) is multiplied by a clutter area to get the sea power.

That clutter area matters. The simulator can use the whole antenna footprint, patch-integrate over that footprint, or use a first-order delay-Doppler resolution cell (Delay-Doppler cell). A smaller assumed cell can lift the modelled ship-to-sea ratio substantially. The detector does not yet verify that a ship anywhere in the footprint shares the reference point’s delay-Doppler bin, so this option is a sensitivity study rather than complete bin-level association.

Finding a ship¶

The ship’s own return comes from its flat sides and its corner (dihedral) structures, which are strong radar reflectors (Targets: base class and ship). Because the ship and the sea share the same path here, they can be compared directly. The simulator forms the signal-to-clutter ratio and the signal-to-clutter-plus-noise ratio,

(6)¶\[\mathrm{SCR} = \frac{P_\mathrm{ship}}{P_\mathrm{ocean}}, \qquad \mathrm{SINR} = \frac{P_\mathrm{ship}}{P_\mathrm{ocean} + N_\mathrm{eff}},\]

where the raw thermal-noise power is

(7)¶\[N = k\,T_\mathrm{sys}\,B,\]

with Boltzmann constant \(k\), system noise temperature \(T_\mathrm{sys}\), and bandwidth \(B\). The detector divides this raw floor by a detection-equivalent coherent/incoherent sensitivity factor before forming \(N_\mathrm{eff}\). The \(\sqrt{M}\) factor represents reduced estimator variance, not reduced mean noise power. A detection is declared when the metric passes the configured threshold.

Whether the implemented metric is noise- or clutter-limited depends on the receiver settings. The \(B\,T_\mathrm{coh}\sqrt{M}\) scaling is useful for comparative sensitivity studies, but without an explicit test statistic, false-alarm probability and fluctuation model it is not a calibrated detection probability.

What you get out¶

Per band, the detection events with their SCR and SINR, plus the per-event power breakdown (ship, sea, noise), as footprint-overlap maps, link-budget breakdown plots, and an optional animation (OUTPUT/Footprint_overlap_backscatter_<CONST>_<band>_<contour>dB.png and OUTPUT/Link_budget_breakdown_backscatter_<CONST>_<band>_*.png). See Moving-target detection.

In area-coverage mode, per-constellation swath-visit maps (OUTPUT/Coverage_grid_<CONST>_backscatter.png plus a combined map). See Coverage.

Where it lives in the code¶

Module

Role in backscatter mode

Backscatter point / BRP

Finds the BRP and the incidence angle for each Tx/Rx pair.

Ocean physics

The two-scale Bragg backscatter that sets the sea clutter level.

Ocean target

Wraps the sea NRCS and the clutter area into a radar cross-section.

Delay-Doppler cell

The delay-Doppler cell that sets the clutter area.

Targets: base class and ship

The ship radar cross-section (flat plates and dihedral corners).

Link budget

The bistatic radar equation behind the ship and sea powers.

Moving-target detection

Matches reflections to the ship and computes the SCR / SINR.

Coverage

Counts near-backscatter swath visits per grid cell (area-coverage mode).

Assumptions and limitations¶

  • Retroreflection geometry. The BRP assumes the transmitter, surface, and receiver are collinear; this is the right point for backscatter, not the forward specular reflection point.

  • Noise- or clutter-limited by settings. The detector applies the configured processing gain to the detection-equivalent thermal scale before forming SINR; the incoherent-look factor is approximate.

  • Bragg gating. The Bragg return is added only near backscatter and at oblique incidence, so the forward path is left unchanged. Out-of-plane polarisation rotation is not yet included.

  • Coarse spatial match. A reflection counts as “on the ship” when the point or its footprint overlaps the ship position.

  • No DDM bin association. Footprint overlap is not proof that ship and ocean reference returns share one delay-Doppler bin.

  • Preliminary absolute RCS. The box/dihedral ship model is useful for aspect trends but is not measurement-calibrated; absolute detection conclusions require an external RCS model or data.

When to use it¶

Use backscatter mode to study ship detection as a radar problem – ship versus sea clutter. It needs the incidence-angle gate as well:

[REFLECTION]
reflection_type = backscatter
max_central_angle_deg = 45.0
max_incidence_angle_deg = 70.0

References¶

  • Valenzuela, G., “Theories for the interaction of electromagnetic and oceanic waves – a review”, Boundary-Layer Meteorology 13, 1978 (Bragg scatter).

  • Gleason, S. & Gebre-Egziabher, D. (eds.), GNSS Applications and Methods, Artech House, 2009.

  • Clarizia, M. P., Braca, P., Ruf, C. S. & Willett, P., “Target detection using GPS signals of opportunity”, Proc. 18th Int. Conf. on Information Fusion (FUSION), Washington, DC, 2015.
